title: Binary search that answers the right question

prereqs.why: This is the algorithm, and the two variants asked for are exactly the ones the standard library provides.
A binary search written without stating its invariant first is a coin flip; with one it is mechanical.
The range is a vector and the bounds are indices into it.

statement:
Input is `n`, then `n` integers in **non-decreasing** order, then `q`, then `q`
query values. Implement these two yourself - do not call `std::lower_bound`,
`bisect` or any equivalent:

- **lower bound**: the first index `i` where `v[i] >= target`, or `n` if there is
  no such index
- **upper bound**: the first index `i` where `v[i] > target`, or `n` if there is
  no such index

For each query print both, and the number of occurrences, which is their
difference.

```
<query> lower <lb> upper <ub> count <ub - lb>
```

```
input:   7                     output:  4 lower 1 upper 4 count 3
         1 4 4 4 7 9 9                  0 lower 0 upper 0 count 0
         4                              5 lower 4 upper 4 count 0
         4 0 5 9                        9 lower 5 upper 7 count 2
```

Both must be O(log n) per query.

### The point of the problem

"Binary search" is usually taught as "find whether x is present", which is the
least useful version. These two answer the question that actually comes up:
**where would it go, and how many are there?** Once you have them, `count` is a
subtraction, "is it present" is `lb < n && v[lb] == target`, and "how many are
below" is `lb` itself.

Note what happens when the target is absent: `lower` and `upper` are equal, and
that common value is the index where the target *would* be inserted to keep the
array sorted. So a single function gives you search and insertion position at
once. That is why the standard library provides these two rather than a `find`.

### Write the invariant down first

Keep a **half-open range** `[lo, hi)` - `lo` included, `hi` excluded - and
maintain this across every pass:

```
every index < lo   has v[index] <  target        (ruled out, too small)
every index >= hi  has v[index] >= target        (ruled out, too big)
the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi)
```

Start with `lo = 0`, `hi = n`, which makes both statements vacuously true, and
loop while `lo < hi`. When the loop ends `lo == hi`, the range holds one
position, and that position is the answer. Every decision inside the loop is
then forced rather than guessed.

Upper bound is the same loop with `<` changed to `<=`. That one character is the
whole difference, and the solution explains why.

### Boundary cases

A target below everything (`lower` 0), above everything (`lower` and `upper` both
`n`), and in a gap between two values. A target equal to the first element and
to the last. An array of all-identical values, where `lower` is 0 and `upper` is
`n`. An empty array, where both are 0. `n = 1`. And duplicates, which are the
entire reason the two functions differ.

### Platform assumptions

Values and queries fit in a 32-bit `int`; `n` is at most 200000 and `q` at most
200000, so an O(n) linear scan per query would be forty billion comparisons and
will time out - the logarithmic version is required, not merely preferred.
Indices are `std::size_t`. `n` is guaranteed non-negative and the input is
guaranteed sorted, so you do not have to check either.
hints: Half-open: `std::size_t lo = 0, hi = v.size();` and `while (lo < hi)`. Nothing is ever `size() - 1`, so an empty array needs no special case and nothing can underflow.

The midpoint is `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`, not `(lo + hi) / 2`. They agree on every input this problem will give you, and the second one overflows on a large enough range - the solution explains the famous case.

Lower bound: if `v[mid] < target` the answer is strictly right of mid, so `lo = mid + 1`; otherwise mid itself is still a candidate, so `hi = mid` (not `mid - 1`). Upper bound: the same loop with `v[mid] <= target`.
